newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Study says 1984 was big year for Colombian drugs.
newsitem.headline: Study says 1984 was big year for Colombian drugs.

text.p: Colombia's drug trade reached a peak in 1984, when narcotics accounted for nearly 98 percent of the country's exports, according to a new study published in a magazine on Sunday.

But the study, which was sponsored by the central bank and a leading economic think-tank, found that earnings from Colombia's trade in illegal drugs were less than many Western drug experts have estimated in the past.
Excerpts of the study were published in Sunday's editions of the weekly news magazine Cambio 16.
Estimates vary widely, but Colombian drug traffickers have been said to make between $3 and $9 billion a year from their trade in cocaine and other illicit drugs.
The new study says those estimates are based more on fiction than fact and that it was only in 1984 that Colombia's income from drug exports exeeded $3 billion.

The study, which is to be published later this month, took eight months to complete and was conducted by a team of economists under the auspices of the Banco de la Republica and Fedesarrollo, Colombia's top private economic think-tank, Cambio 16 said.

It quoted the study as showing that Colombia's net income from the drug trade was $4.1 billion in 1984, when it represented 10.9 percent of the country's gross domestic product and 97.6 percent of all exports.

The economic importance of the drug trade has declined steadily since then, however, and narcotics accounted for just 3.5 percent of GDP in in 1995 and 1996, according to the study. In both those years, illicit drugs represented 23.7 percent of Colombia's total exports, and export revenues from narcotics were estimated at $2.5 billion per year.

The methodolgy of the study was not explained. But Cambio 16 said it was based on more than 70 sources and indicated that 50 percent of all drug shipments have been seized by the authorities since 1990.

It also said it was more profitable to run distribution networks in consumer countries like the United States than to make bulk shipments of drugs from producer countries like Colombia, where operating and production costs have grown steadily in recent years.
"Today, as opposed to the 1980s, the biggest profits are generated through retail sales in consumer countries and not through wholesale sales from Colombia," it said.
Government and anti-narcotics officials could not be reached for comment on the rare study on the profitability of Colombia's drug trade.
But Cambio 16 quoted Col. Leonardo Gallego, head of the anti-narcotics division of Colombia's National Police, as calling it both "great and serious."

Gallego said he had no doubt that people controllng street distribution networks in consumer countries were reaping larger profits than Colombia's wholesale traffickers. This was due, at least in part, to the fact that once powerful drug gangs like Colombia's Cali and Medellin cartels no longer monopolised the supply-side of the business, Gallego said.
